en.hero:
Seeing the world from
a runner's perspective.
en.intro: Not a pro athlete. Not a travel blogger. Just a guy who takes his running shoes everywhere, maps out runs and rates the local running conditions.
en.aboutExcerpt: I’m from Estonia, I work in digital marketing, and I travel with my running shoes.
en.aboutBody:
## Starting point

Growing up in Estonia, I started cross-country skiing as a child. Snowboarding came later, along with a few injuries. By the time I was eighteen, I was spending more time partying, going to the gym only occasionally and sometimes attempting a 2 to 3 km run. (I should point out that I’m no saint now, either: I still enjoy the occasional night out with friends, and there’s room for enjoying life alongside running.)

Around 2018, I remember weighing a little over 100 kg. Then, in 2019, I somehow ended up trying go-kart racing for the first time. It quickly became clear that my weight was a factor, so I set myself a goal: lose 20–25 kg to be more competitive in karting (Rotax DD2 class). And I went all in.

![A kart race and me beside a racing kart in the paddock](/assets/uploads/my-story/karting.jpg "I’m the driver in the black helmet and red kart.")

Eventually, I reached my goal, and things actually went pretty well in karting. As I got fitter, I also started feeling faster on my runs, which eventually led me to running half marathons and full marathons. But then I started having stomach problems during those longer races.

From the beginning of 2025, I decided to make running my main hobby. I could do it almost anywhere, which made it much easier to fit into my everyday and work life. Plus, it was a lot cheaper than karting. :)

## Focus shift

Over the years, stomach pain has become a frustrating part of racing marathons and half marathons. I've now trained for and attempted nine marathons, along with plenty of half marathons, but despite countless visits to the doctor, I still haven't found a clear explanation for why this keeps happening.

After dealing with it for so long, I sometimes wonder whether the invisible stress and anticipation of it happening again might also play a role - It's hard to know for sure. At the same time, shorter distances, especially 10 km, have gone really well. I decided to put marathon goals aside for a while, which left me wondering what the next goal could be.

Then I realised the answer had been right in front of me. I enjoy writing, and I already had routes, photos and memories from the places I have visited over the years with my running shoes. Bringing those experiences together felt like a good new direction. Welcome to Runograph.

## Rocca Sörk: sharing the running

Sharing running with other people was already part of my life before Runograph. In July 2025, I started Rocca Sörk (means Sörk means jog in Estonian language) together with Berit, Birgit and Kristjan. It has since grown quite quickly into a big running community by Estonian standards.

Our regular club run is every Tuesday at 18:30 (Starting point: Rocca Al Mare shopping centre) During the summer season, we also get together for bike rides, and from time to time we organise larger events. It is another part of what I enjoy about running: the people it brings together.

![Rocca Sörk runners warming up and running together, with Markus, Berit, Birgit and Kristjan in the middle photograph](/assets/uploads/my-story/rocca-sork-community.jpg "Rocca Sörk: club runs and events, with me, Berit, Birgit and Kristjan in the middle photo.")

You can find our latest runs, rides and events on [Rocca Sörk’s Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/roccasork/).

## What you will find here

Here on Runograph, I’m collecting the useful parts of my own runs: the routes I actually ran, where I could settle into a rhythm, how safe it felt, what the surface was like and whether I would go back. The scores are my personal impressions of the running, and the maps make it easier to see which parts might suit your own trip.

I will keep adding places as I revisit old memories and take my shoes somewhere new.
